title: Exact solution of a boundary-driven transverse-field Ising model with hidden time-reversal symmetry
abstract: The dissipative transverse-field Ising (TFI) model provides a paradigmatic setting for nonequilibrium quantum many-body physics. We show that a class of boundary-driven TFI models subject to dissipation at only one boundary possesses hidden time-reversal symmetry, which enables an exact construction of their nonequilibrium steady states. The solution admits a matrix-product representation and defines a nonequilibrium partition function from which steady-state observables can be evaluated efficiently. We use the exact solution to characterize the microscopic structure of the steady state through its z-magnetization and two-point correlations. A striking feature is that the local field at the dissipative boundary governs the spatial organization of the steady state throughout the chain. The steady state typically exhibits boundary-localized magnetization profiles and exponentially decaying correlations, whose characteristic length scales are set by the dissipative boundary. In the weak-driving limit, suitably tuned boundary fields can reorganize the NESS into a delocalized single-interface structure, giving rise to long-range correlations that decay linearly with distance.
summary: This paper provides an exact solution for the Nonequilibrium Steady State (NESS) of a boundary-driven transverse-field Ising model by exploiting a hidden time-reversal symmetry. The method constructs the NESS using a Matrix-Product Operator (MPO) representation, showing that the steady-state properties, such as magnetization and correlations, are dictated by the local field at the dissipative boundary. This offers a powerful analytical tool for understanding non-equilibrium quantum dynamics.
main_problem: Determining the Nonequilibrium Steady State (NESS) of open quantum systems, which is generally a formidable numerical task.
main_result: The NESS can be exactly constructed due to the presence of hidden time-reversal symmetry, leading to an MPO representation and revealing boundary-governed spatial organization.
method: The solution utilizes the concept of Hidden Time-Reversal Symmetry (HTRS) by constructing an exactly solvable doubled system whose pure steady state purifies the original system's NESS.
model_or_system: The system is a 1D boundary-driven transverse-field Ising (TFI) model, whose dynamics are governed by a Lindblad master equation incorporating nearest-neighbor interactions, a transverse field, and boundary dissipation.
important_parameters: Boundary fields ($h_L, h_R$), dissipation rate ($\gamma$), and the weak-driving limit where long-range correlations can emerge.
main_assumptions: The model possesses Hidden Time-Reversal Symmetry (HTRS), which is the key mathematical property enabling the exact solution.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic domain and bond structure of the NESS for small chains, and the matrix-product representation of the steady state.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model and the difficulty of finding the NESS, then introduces the HTRS to construct an exactly solvable doubled system. The core methodology involves deriving recurrence relations for the coefficients, leading to the final MPO representation of the NESS, followed by analyzing the resulting spatial correlations in different parameter regimes.
why_interesting: This work provides an exact, analytical framework for calculating steady states in complex, driven-dissipative quantum many-body systems, which is a major challenge in AMO and quantum optics.

The physical system A consists of N spins with longitudinal boundary fields and incoherent gain at site N (right). The mirror system B acts as an absorber and is coupled to A via a unidirectional waveguide. (b) Features of HTRS: two time correlators for a small chain N = 5 with parameters h = 0.5, hL = hR = 0.5 and γ = 0.1. It shows a symmetric correlation between X = Heff and Y = √γσ+ N. This symmetry does not hold for general operators (inset: X = σz 1 and Y = σy 2 + 5σz 4).

FIG. 4. Signatures of special steady-state structures in the weak-driving limit of Eq. (45). Here we set h = γ = 10−3. (a) Leading eigenvalue magnitudes |ξ1| and |ξ2| of T as functions of hR for hL = 2. The two magnitudes become equal at hR = ±1. (b) log10⟨m⟩as a function of the boundary longitudinal fields hL and hR for N = 500, where ⟨m⟩is the steady-state magnetization density. The magnetization density is strongly enhanced near hR = 1 and suppressed near hR = −1. In addition, hL = −1 is distinct from other values of hL at hR = ±1.

FIG. 5. Typical steady-state behavior for hR = 1 and hL ̸= −1 in the weak-driving limit. Here we take hL = −2 and set h = γ = 10−3. (a) Magnetization profile ⟨σz j ⟩SS for N = 100. (b) Connected correlation function Cij for N = 2000. The nearly polarized profile and the nearly vanished connected correlations indicate that the NESS approaches an ideal ferromagnetic state, while the small deviations arise from subleading configurations induced by finite h and γ.
